paths.title: Grace and the beginning of Christian life
paths.audience: New believers and Christians revisiting the foundations
paths.purpose: Learn to receive salvation as grace, respond in repentance and faith, and grow with other believers.
paths.preparation: No prior theological reading required. Work through difficult words with a trusted Christian or church leader.
paths.completion: Explain the difference between receiving Christ and earning acceptance, then name one practice of mutual Christian care.

stages.title: Receive grace
stages.purpose: Begin with what God gives before asking what you must achieve.

scripture.why: Places faith, Christ’s redemption and boasting within Paul’s argument.

sermon.why: The courtroom explanation makes justification easier to distinguish from self-improvement.

reading.why: A complete chapter addresses the fear that an unworthy person cannot come to Christ.

stages.reflection: What is the ground of acceptance, and what place does faith have?
stages.practice: Write a two-sentence account of grace without making your progress its price.

stages.title: Respond with repentance and faith
stages.purpose: Consider how turning to Christ changes your relation to sin.

scripture.why: Read Jesus’ call in the setting of his announcement of God’s kingdom.

sermon.why: Explains why the call to repent and believe also gives the troubled hearer warrant to come.

reading.why: Shows why forgiveness and repentance belong together without treating repentance as a payment.

stages.reflection: How does repentance differ from trying to buy forgiveness?
stages.practice: Name one concrete wrong to confess and one faithful response to practice.

stages.title: Grow in new life and fellowship
stages.purpose: Move from an isolated decision toward dependence on the Spirit and mutual care.

scripture.why: Read new birth and believing together within Jesus’ conversation.
Connect access to God with drawing near, hope and encouragement.

sermon.why: Shows how Christian encouragement can become practical care while leaving room for different church arrangements.

reading.why: Keeps the new birth grounded in God’s work and directs the reader to Christ.

stages.reflection: Which duties are in Hebrews, and which group arrangements are proposed ways of practicing them?
stages.practice: Arrange one conversation about Scripture and one act of encouragement in your church.

paths.sequenceRationale: Learn to receive salvation as grace, respond in repentance and faith, and grow with other believers.
paths.pace: Three stages, usually one stage per week; take longer where useful. This is a suggested pace, not measured reading time.

paths.title: Christ and justification in deeper study
paths.audience: Readers ready for sustained doctrinal argument
paths.purpose: Study Christ’s representative work, the meaning of justification, and the evidence of living faith in sequence.
paths.preparation: Begin after the grace path or equivalent grounding. Read the older prose slowly and define terms from the author’s argument.
paths.completion: Distinguish substitution, justification and the fruits of faith without separating salvation from holiness.

stages.title: Christ as the sinless representative
stages.purpose: Establish whose work bears the weight of reconciliation.

scripture.why: Read verse 21 within Paul’s ministry-of-reconciliation argument.

sermon.why: Introduces the contrast between Christ’s personal sinlessness and his bearing of sin.

reading.why: Supplies a longer exegetical argument after the sermon’s explanation.

stages.reflection: How does Owen distinguish bearing sin from becoming morally sinful?
stages.practice: Outline the argument with the biblical wording beside each inference.

stages.title: Justification and sanctification
stages.purpose: Clarify a change in standing before God and a change within the believer.

scripture.why: Examine Paul’s use of Abraham, faith and the forgiveness of sins.

sermon.why: Return to the courtroom illustration now with more precise questions about its scope.

reading.why: Explains the declarative character of justification while distinguishing it from inward renewal.

stages.reflection: Where does the analogy clarify Paul, and where might an analogy oversimplify?
stages.practice: Write separate definitions of justification and sanctification, then explain their relation.

stages.title: Living faith and obedient action
stages.purpose: Test whether your account can take James’s warning seriously.

scripture.why: Follow James’s examples and his contrast between dead and living faith.

sermon.why: A thematic companion recalls that the gospel calls for repentance as well as belief; it is not a commentary on James.

reading.why: Offers Owen’s sustained reconciliation of Paul and James for evaluation against both texts.

stages.reflection: Does Owen distinguish the ground of acceptance from its evidence convincingly?
stages.practice: Explain his position fairly, then identify the strongest question you would ask him.

paths.sequenceRationale: Study Christ’s representative work, the meaning of justification, and the evidence of living faith in sequence.
paths.pace: Three stages, usually one stage per week; take longer where useful. This is a suggested pace, not measured reading time.

paths.title: Scripture miracles and resurrection
paths.audience: Christians learning to examine and explain foundational truth claims
paths.purpose: Define the claim, distinguish possibility from evidence, and then examine a specific resurrection argument.
paths.preparation: Use a notebook with separate columns for source statement, author inference and your own question. Read 1 Peter 3:15–16 as a posture for discussion.
paths.completion: Present a claim and its reasons while stating what the evidence does and does not establish.

stages.title: What does inspiration mean
stages.purpose: Understand the doctrine before deciding whether an argument supports it.

scripture.why: Locate inspiration within the passage’s emphasis on salvation, teaching and formation.

sermon.why: Hear the doctrine preached to Christian hearers; the sermon itself says it is not developing external proofs.

reading.why: Clarifies terms that are easily confused in conversations about the Bible.

stages.reflection: Which statements define inspiration, and which would need further evidence for a questioning reader?
stages.practice: Give a fair definition before offering an argument; avoid caricaturing the person who disagrees.

stages.title: Could a miracle occur
stages.purpose: Separate a philosophical objection from a historical investigation.

scripture.why: Read Paul’s resurrection question within his defense before Agrippa.

sermon.why: Its treatment of natural analogies helps separate illustration from proof.

reading.why: Alexander argues that revelation and divine intervention are reasonable if God exists; he states the limit of that argument.

stages.reflection: What must Alexander assume, and what further evidence would establish a particular event?
stages.practice: State the strongest objection to the argument and a reply that does not assume the conclusion.

stages.title: What supports the resurrection claim
stages.purpose: Examine a historical argument without confusing theological importance with proof.

scripture.why: Read Paul’s report, named appearances and reasoning about the consequences of denial.

sermon.why: Explains why the claim is bodily and central to the gospel; it is a later interpretation of the evidence.

reading.why: Lets you inspect Alexander’s use of Paul and early Christian belief rather than merely repeat his conclusion.

stages.reflection: What is directly reported, what is inferred, and which alternative explanation requires examination?
stages.practice: Draft a respectful answer distinguishing Paul’s testimony, Alexander’s inference and your remaining research question.

preparationScripture.why: Sets a posture of gentleness and respect for answering questions.

paths.sequenceRationale: Define the claim, distinguish possibility from evidence, and then examine a specific resurrection argument.
paths.pace: Three stages, usually one stage per week; take longer where useful. This is a suggested pace, not measured reading time.

paths.title: Grief assurance and care at home
paths.audience: Christians facing sorrow or doubt and those accompanying them
paths.purpose: Practice patient listening, ground assurance in Christ, and carry care into ordinary household life.
paths.preparation: Take one stage at a time with someone you trust. These readings offer spiritual companionship, not a complete response to every crisis.
paths.completion: Offer encouragement that neither promises a quick resolution nor makes spiritual confidence a condition of being heard.

stages.title: Make room for sorrow
stages.purpose: Attend to grief before reaching for an explanation of another person’s experience.

scripture.why: Notice bereavement, Naomi’s words and Ruth’s companionship before the later resolution.

sermon.why: Provides a narrative account of grief and mercy to discuss, while requiring care with its applications.

reading.why: An experienced preacher’s admission of weakness resists the assumption that usefulness requires constant emotional strength.

stages.reflection: Which promises can you offer, and which explanations of a particular loss would go beyond what you know?
stages.practice: Listen without correcting the person’s first expression of grief; offer one specific form of practical help.

stages.title: Distinguish weak faith from no faith
stages.purpose: Consider assurance without requiring an unwavering emotional state.

scripture.why: Read the testimony to the Son, the purpose of assurance, and Newton’s main text in context.

sermon.why: Explicitly rejects making full assurance essential to the existence of genuine faith.

reading.why: Directs hope toward God’s faithfulness and union with Christ.

stages.reflection: How can you encourage trust without demanding that someone first feel certain?
stages.practice: Identify one promise in the text and discuss it without measuring faith by the intensity of a feeling.

stages.title: Care through Scripture prayer and example
stages.purpose: Move from general concern to sustained household practices.

scripture.why: Read the household declaration within covenant commitment and the people’s response.

sermon.why: Brings household instruction and prayer into view alongside public worship.

reading.why: Provides sustained counsel on introducing Scripture and prayer to children.

stages.reflection: What can a caregiver faithfully do, and what belongs to God rather than parental control?
stages.practice: Choose a short, sustainable time for Scripture and prayer; readers without children can consider how to support a family without taking over its responsibilities.

paths.sequenceRationale: Practice patient listening, ground assurance in Christ, and carry care into ordinary household life.
paths.pace: Three stages, usually one stage per week; take longer where useful. This is a suggested pace, not measured reading time.

paths.title: Character teaching and mission in ministry
paths.audience: Prospective pastors elders teachers and group leaders
paths.purpose: Put character before technique, learn responsible application, and connect preparation to service and mission.
paths.preparation: Study within the oversight of your church. Completing a path does not establish a call, qualification or office.
paths.completion: Prepare a short passage-based lesson, invite correction, and identify one accountable opportunity to serve.

stages.title: Watch your life and teaching
stages.purpose: Begin with the person who serves rather than a collection of methods.

scripture.why: Hold example, doctrine, public reading and perseverance together.

sermon.why: Connects a pastor’s joy to people walking in truth, rather than the teacher’s prominence.

reading.why: Explains why the minister’s inward life belongs to the work itself.

stages.reflection: What would people who know you well say about the relation between your teaching and conduct?
stages.practice: Ask a trusted church leader for one concrete area of growth and a way to follow it up.

stages.title: Understand before applying
stages.purpose: Learn to explain a passage and address real hearers responsibly.

scripture.why: Read the charge to preach alongside patience, teaching and endurance.

sermon.why: Challenges the equation of frequent reading with genuine understanding.

reading.why: Shows how application takes account of hearers while preserving the relation of law and gospel.

stages.reflection: Does your application arise from the passage, and how would it differ for two different hearers?
stages.practice: Prepare a ten-minute lesson with a text summary, main claim and two reasoned applications; invite review.

stages.title: Serve and participate in mission
stages.purpose: Let preparation lead to faithful witness in cooperation with others.

scripture.why: Read disciple-making under Christ’s authority and promised presence.

sermon.why: Joins character and intentional witness, rather than treating evangelism as technique alone.

reading.why: Provides a substantial historical argument for continuing obligation and shared practical means.

stages.reflection: Which parts of Carey’s proposal express an enduring obligation, and which are context-dependent methods?
stages.practice: Plan one act of service or witness with your church, including whom to learn from and how to evaluate it.

paths.sequenceRationale: Put character before technique, learn responsible application, and connect preparation to service and mission.
paths.pace: Three stages, usually one stage per week; take longer where useful. This is a suggested pace, not measured reading time.
